title: Spatial, broad-window, lagged and trend temperature terms fitted before 2005 did not forecast the 2005-2024 level shift that interannual slopes missed in 149 Swiss plant and UK butterfly series
abstract: Question: earlier campaign forward tests found that frozen climate-response relations track year-to-year variation but miss the later multi-year level of the response. Can a sensitivity estimated from training years alone forecast this missed level? Approach: a plan frozen and timestamped before fitting. 149 units: 66 MeteoSwiss plant phases, 43 UK butterfly species (mean flight date) and 40 species (log site index), with E-OBS temperature of each site's grid cell. Training up to 2004, test 2005-2024; second split at 1994. Against the usual interannual model (selected 1-3 month window), we tested a spatial slope (space-for-time), a broad window, all-month ridge, 5-year temperature memory, a spatial/interannual hybrid and the training trend. Rule: a mechanism explains the missed shift if the median missed shift falls by half and skill improves in most units. Results: the interannual model missed shifts with the sign of the observed shift in 52/66, 42/43 and 36/40 units (median shifts -3.0 days, -4.1 days, -0.15 ln units; 60%, 9% and 11% forecast). No pre-registered mechanism met the rule in any system or split. Spatial and interannual slopes were almost equal (median ratio 1.04 and 0.94). Exploratory checks: homogenised station temperature (NBCN, HadCET) gave the same warming. UK butterfly windows warmed only 0.15 C relative to the site training means, so the 4.1-day advance would need about ten times the interannual sensitivity. A daily thermal-time model forecast a median 83% of the Swiss plant shift (65% for the interannual model; better skill in 36 of 46 units; 92% in the second split) but only 20% of the butterfly shift. A trailing 5-year level plus the frozen climate anomaly gave the best skill against the training mean in all systems (0.48, 0.11, 0.24 against 0.19, 0.04, -0.03) and beat the interannual model in 66/66, 33/43 and 39/40 units. Interpretation: the missed plant level is mostly model form; the butterfly level is mostly not a temperature response in these data. A level update is the robust forecast practice. Limitations: exploratory analyses chosen after the main results; units share years and climate; UKBMS metric and recording changes were not tested; source data are not bundled (retrieval script and hashes given).

display.caption: Median absolute missed level shift in 2005-2024 for each model in three systems. Filled points are pre-registered models; open points are exploratory. No pre-registered climate mechanism reached the dotted line (half of the interannual model). The trailing level models (R2, R2I) gave the smallest missed shifts.

(a) Observed level shift against site-weighted warming of the selected window; dashed lines show the median interannual slope. UK butterflies advanced about 4 days with about 0.15 C of warming. (b) Fraction of the shift forecast by an exploratory daily thermal-time model against the interannual window model.

citations.reason: Tests the climate explanations of the level shifts that this synthesis found, and confirms its level-update model in 149 new unit-level tests.
Reuses its data preparation code and data sources; examines why its frozen relations forecast only part of the 2005-2024 phenology advance.
Our exploratory thermal-time model also describes Swiss plant responses to warming better than linear window models.
